newsitem.title: USA: Soybeans soar on export rumors, coffee up.
newsitem.headline: Soybeans soar on export rumors, coffee up.

text.p: Soybean prices soared on Tuesday on rumors that a recent sharp drop in prices was sparking fresh interest from China and other overseas buyers.

In other markets, coffee prices rose on a surprisingly low estimate of Brazil's crop by a U.S. Agriculture Department specialist. Gold prices held above Monday's 12-year lows and oil prices were firm as traders expected a drop in gasoline stocks due to last week's holiday driving.
At the Chicago Board of Trade, soybeans for July delivery closed 35-1/4 cents a bushel higher at $7.68.
"With the kind of beating the soybeans have taken we have now priced ourselves comparably to South America," said Dave Maher, analyst with Securities Corp of Iowa.

Soybean prices hit an 8-1/2 year high at $9.03-1/2 on May 9 as processors and exporters fought for dwindling supplies of last year's crop. But huge soybean plantings this spring and ideal weather in the Midwest have begun pointing to a record crop this year.
News last month that some firms such as Minneapolis-based Cargill Inc were importing Brazilian soybeans to tide themselves over until the fall harvest also pressured prices.

But rumors were rampant early on Tuesday that China bought U.S. soybeans, along with other rumors of fresh sales to Europe. There was also talk that processors in Brazil -- the second largest soybean exporter -- were looking for U.S. soybeans.
The rally in soybeans aided corn prices, and July corn closed up 2-3/4 cents a bushel at $2.43-1/4.

Prices rose after an influential consultant, Sparks Companies of Memphis, Tenn., estimated 1997 U.S. corn production at only 9.48 billion bushels. That was below last month's Agriculture Department estimate of 9.84 billion and some other private forecasts for up to 10 billion bushels.
"The corn number is pretty low considering how well everything looks," Ron Kucha, CBOT floor broker for O'Connor and Co, said of the Sparks estimate.
Wheat prices, which hit a three-year low on Monday amid active harvesting and good yields from winter wheat, closed higher on the firmness in other grains.
July wheat closed up 3 cents a bushel at $3.16-1/2.

In New York, gold took a breather from the recent heavy selling that drove prices to 12-year lows on Monday. But analysts said the steadiness might not last long. Gold for August delivery closed up $2.00 an ounce at $321.00.

"Gold is way oversold technically, so a bounce was not a surprise, and funds are likely to take profits on short positions from time to time," said Refco analyst James Steel. "But the market remains bearish, given the likelihood of more central bank activity."

On Monday, spot gold was fixed at $318.75, its lowest level since December 1985, after news late last week that Australia's central bank had sold about two-thirds of its gold reserves in the past six months.

At the Coffee Sugar and Cocoa Exchange in New York, coffee was jolted by a surprisingly small estimate for this year's Brazil coffee crop by the U.S. Agriculture Department. Coffee for July delivery closed up 6.25 cents a pound at 191.50 cents.

The report by the department's attache in Brazil, dated May 9, put Brazil's harvest at 24 million 132-pound bags, down sharply from the Department's estimate of 28 million bags published in its June report.

"Four million bags is a big difference," said Hencorp Becstone president Victor Henriquez. "Those four million bags could represent the difference between a price for coffee of 150 or 250 (cents)" in the September futures, he said.

Coffee hit 20-year highs at 318 cents a pound in early May on panic over tight supplies, poor crops in Latin America and worries about a possible frost in Brazil in June and July. Those concerns had steadily eased with mild weather in Brazil.

Mario Conti, a director of key roaster Nestle AG, said on Tuesday he expected continued volatility in world coffee markets and cautioned that price hikes were hurting consumption -- especially in the United States and central Europe.
"Some sources presently estimate that North American consumption volume might drop by as much as 10 percent in 1997 compared to 1996," Conti told coffee traders in Colombia.
Oil prices closed higher led by gasoline on expectations that weekly oil inventory data would show a drop in gasoline supplies due to Fourth of July holiday driving.
Gasoline for August delivery ended 0.98 cent up at 58.92 cents a gallon, while August crude ended 21 cents a barrel higher at $19.73 and August heating oil up 0.22 cent a gallon at 53.00 cents.
Dealers said American Petroleum Institute data due on Tuesday afternoon would likely show a draw of one to two million barrels in gasoline stocks.
"Gasoline clearly led the complex today with the market expecting a decent API report due to Fourth of July demand," said John Saucer, analyst with Smith Barney in Houston.
